title: Prediction and entropy of printed English

nodes.text: A new method of estimating the entropy and redundancy of a language exploits a native speaker's implicit knowledge of language statistics by measuring how well they can predict the next letter given the preceding text.
nodes.evidence: A new method of estimating the entropy and redundancy of a language is described. This method exploits the knowledge of the language statistics possessed by those who speak the language

nodes.text: The N-gram entropy F_N is defined as the conditional entropy of the next letter given the preceding N-1 letters, and the true entropy H of a language is the limiting value of F_N as N approaches infinity.
Considering statistical effects extending over not more than eight letters, the entropy of English is roughly 2.3 bits per letter with a redundancy of about 50 percent.
nodes.evidence: It was estimated that when statistical effects extending over not more than eight letters are considered the entropy is roughly 2.3 bits per letter, the redundancy about 50 per cent.

nodes.text: Long-range statistical effects up to 100 letters reduce the entropy of ordinary literary English to roughly one bit per letter, corresponding to a redundancy of about 75 percent.
nodes.evidence: the long range statistical effects (up to 100 letters) reduce the entropy to something of the order of one bit per letter, with a corresponding redundancy of roughly 75%

nodes.text: Direct calculation from letter statistics gives a 26-letter-alphabet zero-order entropy F0 of 4.70 bits, single-letter F1 = 4.14 bits, digram F2 = 3.56 bits, and trigram F3 = 3.3 bits per letter.
nodes.evidence: F1 = 4.14 bits per letter ... F2 = 7.70 - 4.14 = 3.56 bits per letter ... F3 = 11.0 - 7.7 = 3.3

nodes.text: English word probabilities follow Zipf's law p_n = k/n (probability inversely proportional to frequency rank), which gives a good approximation across many different languages.
nodes.evidence: Zipf has pointed out that this type of formula, p_n = k/n, gives a rather good approximation to the word probabilities in many different languages.

nodes.text: Using word frequencies and a Zipf distribution truncated at rank 8,727, the per-word entropy is 11.82 bits per word, equivalent to about 2.62 bits per letter at an average word length of 4.5 letters.
nodes.evidence: the entropy is then: 11.82 bits per word, or 11.82/4.5 = 2.62 bits per letter since the average word length in English is 4.5 letters

nodes.text: A prediction experiment in which a subject guesses successive letters of an unfamiliar passage, being told only whether each guess is right, yields a reduced text that contains the same information as the original and can in principle be inverted using an identical (mathematical) twin predictor.
nodes.evidence: both lines contain the same information in the sense that it is possible, at least in principle, to recover the first line from the second. To accomplish this we need an identical twin of the individual

nodes.text: In a single-guess prediction experiment, a subject correctly guessed 89 of 129 letters (69%), with errors concentrated at the beginnings of words and syllables where the line of thought can branch.
nodes.evidence: Of a total of 129 letters, 89 or 69% were guessed correctly. The errors, as would be expected, occur most frequently at the beginning of words and syllables

nodes.text: The reduced text can be regarded as an encoded version of the original produced by passing it through a reversible transducer, so a communication system could transmit only the reduced text between two identical prediction devices.
nodes.evidence: the reduced text can be considered to be an encoded form of the original, the result of passing the original text through a reversible transducer

nodes.text: Reverse prediction (guessing the letter preceding known text) scored only slightly worse than forward prediction, and the N-gram entropy F_N for a reversed language equals that of the forward language.
nodes.evidence: the N-gram entropy FN for a reversed language is equal to that for the forward language ... the scores were only slightly poorer

nodes.text: The prediction-based encoding makes redundancy explicit: it translates the original 27-symbol alphabet into a new alphabet (guess numbers 1..27) with highly unequal symbol probabilities, where symbol 1 has very high frequency, which is what enables entropy estimation from the experiments.
nodes.evidence: The redundancy which originally appeared in complicated constraints among groups of letters, has, by the translating process, been made explicit to a large extent in the very unequal probabilities of the new symbols.
